title: Balance a Binary Search Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: AVL-style rotation rebalancing versus flattening via in-order traversal and rebuilding using the middle-as-root technique.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given the root of a (possibly unbalanced) binary search tree, return a height-balanced BST containing the same values. Any valid balanced BST is acceptable.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Rebalance an arbitrary BST\"","In-order traversal gives sorted values regardless of the original tree's shape; rebuild balanced from that sorted list"],["This reduces directly to Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree","The same middle-as-root divide-and-conquer construction applies once the values are flattened"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Regardless of how skewed the input BST is, its in-order traversal always produces the same sorted sequence of values. This means the entire problem reduces to: flatten the tree via in-order traversal to get a sorted array, then apply the well-known middle-as-root technique to build a balanced BST from it.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reorganizing a Messy Bookshelf Sorted by Title into a Balanced Display
blocks.text: Picture a bookshelf where books are technically in alphabetical order but oddly and unevenly stacked. Simply reading off all the titles in order (flattening), then rebuilding a neat, evenly-tiered display by always placing the middle title on each new tier, produces a balanced arrangement regardless of how messy the original stacking was.

blocks.caption: In-order traversal flattens the tree to a sorted list; rebuild balanced using the middle-as-root technique

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: root = [1,null,2,null,3,null,4,null,null] (a fully right-skewed chain 1->2->3->4)
Result (preorder): 2 1 null null 3 null 4 null null, a balanced tree containing 1,2,3,4.
5. How Should We Think?

Before attempting complex tree rotations to rebalance in place, notice that flattening the tree to its sorted values (via in-order traversal) and rebuilding it using the SAME middle-as-root technique as Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree directly and simply solves this problem.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In-order traversal of ANY BST (balanced or not) always produces the same sorted sequence of its values.

Observation 2: Once this sorted sequence is obtained, building a balanced BST from it is EXACTLY the well-known Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree problem: pick the middle element as root, recurse on both halves.

Observation 3: This completely bypasses any need for in-place tree rotation algorithms (like AVL or red-black tree rebalancing), which are considerably more complex.

Observation 4: The result is guaranteed height-balanced, since the middle-as-root construction always splits remaining elements as evenly as possible.
This leads to flattening the tree via in-order traversal to get a sorted array, then rebuilding a balanced BST from it using the middle-as-root recursive construction.
6. Brute Force Solution
Attempt to rebalance the tree in place using tree rotation operations (as in AVL tree rebalancing), repeatedly rotating until height balance is achieved everywhere.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Tree rotations directly rebalance in place without ever flattening the tree.
Correctly implementing rotation-based rebalancing (as in AVL trees) is considerably more complex and error-prone than the flatten-and-rebuild approach.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n) for AVL-style rebalancing in the general case.
Space: O(height) for rotation operations.
Limitation: while asymptotically similar, rotation-based rebalancing is significantly more complex to implement correctly than simply flattening and rebuilding.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Since in-order traversal always produces the same sorted values regardless of the tree's shape, and the middle-as-root construction is a well-understood, simple technique for building a balanced BST from sorted data, combining these two ideas solves the problem directly without any need for rotation logic.
Flatten the tree via in-order traversal into a sorted array. Recursively build a new tree: pick the middle index as root, recurse on the left and right sub-ranges.

Why This Works

In-order traversal correctly recovers the sorted sequence of values regardless of the original tree's shape, and the middle-as-root recursive construction is a proven technique guaranteeing O(log n) height, since it always divides remaining elements as evenly as possible. Combining these two well-understood techniques solves the rebalancing problem simply and correctly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for the values array, O(log n) recursion depth for the rebuild.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Balance a Binary Search Tree is a great example of recognizing that a seemingly hard "rebalancing" problem reduces directly to two simpler, well-known techniques: in-order flattening and Sorted-Array-to-BST reconstruction.
Common Mistakes

items: Attempting complex rotation-based rebalancing when the simpler flatten-and-rebuild approach solves the problem directly.
Forgetting that any valid balanced BST is acceptable, not just one specific "canonical" answer.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "this reduces to Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree once flattened via in-order traversal" demonstrates strong problem-reduction skills.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "rebalance an arbitrary BST", think: flatten via in-order traversal, rebuild using the middle-as-root technique.
Interview Follow-up Questions

12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: reduce rebalancing to two known techniques: in-order flattening, then Sorted-Array-to-BST reconstruction.
Core Idea: flatten the tree via in-order traversal into a sorted array, then rebuild using the middle-as-root recursive technique.
Time: O(n log n) for rotation-based rebalancing, O(n) for the flatten-and-rebuild approach.
Most Important Observation: in-order traversal always recovers the same sorted values, regardless of the tree's original shape.
Interview Difficulty: a satisfying reduction problem connecting two previously-seen techniques.
One line memory trick: flatten via in-order, rebuild via middle-as-root.
